To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) VFO is generated by principal neurons, and occurs at the interface between epileptic and normal tissue; (b) VFO is a consequence of the interaction of excitatory and inhibitory synapses on principal neurons, and is therefore a measure of the relative strengths of these synapses; (c) VFO can be used to identify the epileptogenic focus in the brain, and can be used to predict the efficacy of anticonvulsant therapy; and (d)
VFO in vitro are gap-junction-generated, and that they may be the key to understanding the mechanisms of seizures.

1) VFO are a normal, physiologically relevant brain rhythm, 2) VFO are generated by principal neuron axons that are coupled by gap junctions, 3) VFO occur in the absence of synaptic transmission, 4) VFO are suppressed by synaptic activity, 5) VFO are facilitated by high pH and low Ca(2+) and 6) VFO are associated with seizure networks.
